items.title: George Guesnon Interview, 1965-09
items.q: The name 'Marrero' is mentioned by the Interviewer in a comparison ('Geno is much better than Marrero') regarding drumming styles. The Interviewee does not mention Marrero, nor does he confirm or deny any personal relationship, only agreeing with the general sentiment that the comparison is 'quite t

ctx.x: Well, I mean, he's a young son, but he started on Emmanuel Perez. He did? Yeah, yeah. He's good, I mean, you know, but he's not a jazz musician. No? He's one of the greatest musicians in New Orleans. He arranges, composes, right now he just says something, write something for twelve pieces. He put it on paper for a twelve piece band, ten piece band. Yeah? Yeah. Writer Ramers. He's a great musician, but he just can't. You know, he ain't no great jazz man, you know? In other words, he's been in the big bands around…

he say, I'd go to Duke Ellington's band. I like this. From the Eureka magazine. A much more satisfactory four-four beat, as is the playing of, in the LP under Robinson's name. Geno is much better than Marrero. His rhythm playing is lighter and harder for him. Yeah, I think what I'm sure. And he plays jazz solos, well constructed and melodic.

That's quite true. Well, I mean, well the Cressnos, like I say, you seek for more, you find more. I mean, Lawrence, I mean, I tried to break him with that. It became too much of a monotonous thing. Everything was too, heavy. And it just never, the change never stroked. You know what I mean? The stroke never changed. I mean, it was, you see, but you don't have to play like that. Instead of trying, you judge from your wrist. Uh-huh. Of what you must do. When they become loud, when they get soft. Yeah. That's right.…
